meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I really didn't say everything I said'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine, not apocryphal: Berra said it to Newsday in February 1986. It's the four rewritten variants in circulation that have weak evidence.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: 1925–2015 · Hall of Fame catcher, New York Yankees
answer.sourceLine: Genuine — and unusually well documented for a Berra line. Quote Investigator ↗ finds good evidence that Berra said this exact wording as recorded in Newsday on 24 February 1986, when he was a new coach with the Houston Astros; he later made it the subtitle of his own collection, The Yogi Book: I Really Didn’t Say Everything I Said! (Workman Publishing, 1998).

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: The Yogi Book: I Really Didn’t Say Everything I Said!
Yogi Berra (1925–2015), then a coach with the Houston Astros

source.excerpt: “I really didn’t say everything I said,” Berra said, creating another original.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ lists five circulating wordings and finds good evidence for exactly one of them — this one — recorded in Newsday on 24 February 1986 in a profile by Steve Marcus.
Wikiquote ↗ carries the line in its sourced “Yogiisms” section, cited to Berra’s own book — not in its attributed or misattributed lists.

Berra put the sentence on his own cover: Open Library’s edition record ↗ gives the full title as The Yogi book: I really didn’t say everything I said!, Workman Publishing, 1998, 127 pages, ISBN 0761110909.

A syndicated column by Murray Olderman, published 2 December 1975 — Quote Investigator ↗ cites it in the Bowling Green, Kentucky, Daily News, page 15 — had already told readers Berra “never said most of those ‘funnies’” and that Joe Garagiola made them up for him. That is the kind of claim Berra’s line answers.
source.excerptNote: As transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗ from Steve Marcus’s Newsday profile of 24 February 1986. Wikiquote ↗ quotes a fuller version from The Yogi Book, which continues: “Then again, I might have said ’em, but you never know.”

source.rightsNote: This is a twentieth-century American remark and both documented sources for it are modern. The Newsday report that first records the wording was published on 24 February 1986, and The Yogi Book was published by Workman Publishing in 1998 — both far later than the pre-1931 line for United States public domain, so both remain in copyright. The seven-word sentence itself is quoted here for identification and comment.

author.name: Yogi Berra
author.heading: About the speaker
author.metaLine: 1925–2015 · Hall of Fame catcher and manager, New York Yankees
author.bio: Lawrence Peter “Yogi” Berra (1925–2015) caught for the New York Yankees from 1946 to 1963 and was elected to the Baseball Hall of Fame in 1972. He went on to manage the Yankees and the Mets, and was coaching the Houston Astros when he said this line. His tangled, circular one-liners — the Yogi-isms — grew so famous that people began inventing new ones and crediting them to him, which is precisely what this quote is complaining about.

misattribution.heading: The variants with weak evidence
misattribution.intro: The joke here folds in on itself: this quote is real, and it is the other four versions of it — the ones people actually repeat — that keep getting put in Berra’s mouth with little behind them. Quote Investigator ↗ lists five wordings in circulation and finds good evidence for only the first.

items.why: Quote Investigator ↗ records this shortened form in Baseball Anecdotes by Daniel Okrent and Steve Wulf (Oxford University Press, 1989), and rates the support for versions other than the 1986 wording as weak. Note that it is simply the 1986 sentence with “really” dropped — most likely a loose rendering of the line Berra is documented saying rather than a separate remark.

items.who: “Half the things I said, I never said them”
items.why: Quote Investigator ↗ traces this form to a New York Times piece by Joe Sharkey on 19 May 1996 — ten years after the wording Berra is documented saying.

items.who: “I never said most of the things I said”
items.why: Quote Investigator ↗ records this form in Steven Pinker’s Words and Rules (HarperCollins, 2000). A related third-person phrasing, “he never said half the things he said,” appears in a 1995 book QI also cites.

A syndicated Murray Olderman column of 2 December 1975 — Quote Investigator ↗ cites it in the Bowling Green, Kentucky, Daily News — told readers Berra “never said most of those ‘funnies’” and that “Joe Garagiola made them up for him.” QI notes only that Garagiola, Berra’s teammate and friend, “enjoyed telling colorful yarns that mixed fact and fiction” — it does not endorse the column’s sweeping claim.

misattribution.truthLine: Berra really did say it. Quote Investigator ↗ finds good evidence for the exact wording “I really didn’t say everything I said” in Newsday on 24 February 1986, and he later made it the subtitle of his own book — so if you are going to quote him on fake quotes, use the real one.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: By February 1986 Berra had left the Yankees dugout and turned up in a Houston Astros uniform, and the reporter sent to profile him found the same scene that had followed Berra for thirty years: a crowd waiting for him to say something quotable. According to the passage Quote Investigator ↗ transcribes, fans hung on his every word hoping for a Berra-ism — many of which, the paper noted, had been said by others and pinned on Yogi. His reply was this line.

That makes it a rare thing: a genuine quotation whose subject is fake quotations. Berra spent decades being handed other people’s wisecracks, and instead of denying them one by one he produced a sentence that swallows its own tail. He liked it enough to put it on the cover of a book.
context.detailsSummary: Berra kept working the same joke
detailsBody: He returned to the theme for the rest of his life. Asked about “It ain’t over till the fat lady sings,” he told the New York Times in 1998: “That’s one of the things that I said that I never said,” as Wikipedia ↗ records.

The suspicion he was answering was old and public. A syndicated column by Murray Olderman of 2 December 1975 — Quote Investigator ↗ cites it in the Bowling Green, Kentucky, Daily News — flatly told readers that Berra “never said most of those ‘funnies’” and that his teammate Joe Garagiola “made them up for him.”
context.pull: “Then again, I might have said ’em, but you never know.”
